title: The alphabet, accents and spelling: ça s'écrit comment ?
summary: Say the 26 letters the French way, read and write the accents, and spell a name or an e-mail address aloud.
focus: Saying the letters, using the accents and spelling words aloud
content:
## The 26 letters

Same 26 letters as English, said the French way. Many are close to English: **B** (bay), **C** (say), **D** (day), **F** (eff), **L** (ell), **M** (em), **N** (en), **O** (oh), **P** (pay), **S** (ess), **T** (tay), **V** (vay), **Z** (zed).

Learn these:

| letter | said | letter | said |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | ah | **K** | kah |
| **E** | euh | **Q** | kü |
| **I** | ee | **R** | air, from the throat |
| **G** | zhay | **U** | ü (*ee* with round lips) |
| **J** | zhee | **W** | double v |
| **H** | ash | **X** | eeks |
| | | **Y** | i grec (Greek i) |

Traps: **G** and **J** swap easily, and French **I** sounds like English *E*.

## Accents and what they change

An accent is part of the spelling.

| accent | name | example |
|---|---|---|
| **é** | accent aigu | **le café**: a closed *ay* |
| **è** | accent grave | **le père**: an open *eh* |
| **ê** | accent circonflexe | **la fête**: open *eh*, like è |
| **à**, **ù** | accent grave | **à**, **où**: the sound stays the same |
| **ç** | cédille | **ça**, **le garçon**: the c says *s* before a, o, u |
| **ë**, **ï** | tréma | **Noël**: say the two vowels apart |

Some only tell two words apart:

- **ou** (or) / **où** (where): **Du thé ou du café ?** / **Où est Marie ?**
- **a** (has) / **à** (to, at, in): **Il a un chat.** / **Il habite à Paris.**

## Silent letters and nasal vowels

French writes letters it does not say.

- A final **e** is silent: **la table**, **Marie**.
- Most final consonants are silent: **Paris**, **petit**, **grand**, **les**, **le prix**.
- But **c, r, f, l** at the end are often heard: **avec**, **bonjour**, **neuf**, **il**. Think *CaReFuL*.
- **h** is never heard: **l'hôtel**, **le thé**.

An **n** or **m** after a vowel often makes a *nasal* vowel, said through the nose with no full n at the end:

| spelling | examples |
|---|---|
| **an**, **en** | **la France**, **l'enfant** |
| **on** | **bonjour**, **non** |
| **in**, **ain** | **le vin**, **le pain** |
| **un** | **un**, **lundi** |

## Spelling it out: ça s'écrit comment ?

To ask how a word is spelled: **Ça s'écrit comment ?** or **Comment ça s'écrit ?** More formally: **Vous pouvez épeler, s'il vous plaît ?** The answer: **Ça s'écrit L, E, F, E accent grave, V, R, E.**

While you spell, you say:

- **majuscule** / **minuscule**: capital / lower-case (**un M majuscule**)
- **deux l** (or **double l**): **Isabelle**
- **e accent aigu**, **c cédille**, **i tréma**
- **tiret** (hyphen): **Jean-Luc** = J, E, A, N, tiret, L, U, C
- **apostrophe**: **aujourd'hui** = … D, apostrophe, H, U, I

In an e-mail address, **@** is **arobase** and **.** is **point**: **paul.morel@mail.fr** = *paul point morel arobase mail point f r*. Addresses take no accents.

vocabulary.example: Le mot café prend un accent aigu.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The word café takes an acute accent.

vocabulary.example: Père s'écrit avec un accent grave.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Père is spelled with a grave accent.

vocabulary.example: Garçon s'écrit avec une cédille.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Garçon is spelled with a cedilla.

vocabulary.example: Paris prend une majuscule.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Paris takes a capital letter.

vocabulary.example: Les jours de la semaine s'écrivent en minuscules.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The days of the week are written in lower case.

vocabulary.example: Vous pouvez épeler votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?
vocabulary.example_meaning: Can you spell your name, please?

vocabulary.example: Thomas, ça s'écrit avec un h.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Thomas is spelled with an h.

vocabulary.example: Jean-Luc s'écrit avec un tiret.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Jean-Luc is written with a hyphen.

vocabulary.example: Il y a une arobase dans chaque adresse e-mail.
vocabulary.example_meaning: There's an at sign in every e-mail address.

vocabulary.example: Mon adresse finit par point f r.
vocabulary.example_meaning: My address ends in dot f r.

quiz.prompt: Which letter does a French speaker say as 'zhay' (zh as in 'measure')?
quiz.explanation: G is said zhay and J is said zhee, the opposite of what English speakers expect. H is said ash.
hints: The letter J ends in an ee sound.
Think of the vowel at the end: zh-ay.

quiz.prompt: Tu habites ___ ? (Where do you live?) Write ou or où.
quiz.explanation: Où with a grave accent means 'where'; ou without it means 'or'. In writing, the accent is the only difference.

quiz.prompt: J'habite ___ Lyon. (I live in Lyon.) Write a or à.
quiz.explanation: À with a grave accent means 'in, at, to' before a city. A without the accent is the verb 'has' (il a un chat).

quiz.prompt: Why does 'garçon' have a cedilla under the c?
options: So the c sounds like s before the o
So the c sounds like k
So the c is not pronounced
quiz.correct_answer: So the c sounds like s before the o
quiz.explanation: Before a, o or u, a plain c sounds like k (le café). The cedilla turns it into an s sound: ça, le garçon, François.
hints: Say 'gar-kon' and 'gar-son': which one is the French word?

quiz.prompt: The first letter of the name 'Élodie' carries an accent grave.
quiz.explanation: É carries an accent aigu: the stroke rises to the right and the vowel sounds like 'ay'. The accent grave leans the other way: è.
hints: Aigu rises to the right: é. Grave falls to the right: è.

quiz.prompt: — Martin, ___ s'écrit comment ? — M, A, R, T, I, N.
quiz.explanation: Ça s'écrit comment ? asks how something is spelled. The c of ça needs its cedilla.
hints: A two-letter word with a cedilla.

quiz.prompt: Isabelle s'écrit avec ___ l. (Isabelle is spelled with two l's.)
quiz.explanation: A doubled letter is spelled deux l (or double l): I, S, A, B, E, deux l, E.

quiz.prompt: How do you read the address 'lea.roux@poste.fr' aloud in French?
options: lea point roux arobase poste point f r
lea tiret roux arobase poste point f r
lea point roux tiret poste point f r
quiz.correct_answer: lea point roux arobase poste point f r
quiz.explanation: @ is arobase and every dot is point; fr is read letter by letter: f r.
hints: The dot and the @ have different names.

quiz.prompt: When you spell 'Wagner' in French, you say the W as 'double v'.
quiz.explanation: French calls W double v (double vé): a doubled V, where English sees a doubled U.
hints: English says 'double u'; French looks at the letter differently.

listening.text: Votre nom, ça s'écrit comment ?
listening.meaning: Your name: how is it spelled?
listening.note: Ça s'écrit comment ? asks for the spelling.

listening.text: Vous pouvez épeler votre prénom ?
listening.meaning: Can you spell your first name?
listening.note: New word: le prénom = the first name.

listening.text: Le mot fête prend un accent circonflexe.
listening.meaning: The word fête takes a circumflex accent.
listening.note: New word: le mot = the word.

listening.text: Mère et père prennent un accent grave.
listening.meaning: Mère and père take a grave accent.

listening.text: Écrivez votre nom en majuscules, s'il vous plaît.
listening.meaning: Write your name in capitals, please.

listening.text: Mon nom de famille s'écrit avec un tiret.
listening.meaning: My surname is written with a hyphen.
listening.note: New word: le nom de famille = the surname.

listening.text: Dans une adresse e-mail, on dit arobase et point.
listening.meaning: In an e-mail address, you say arobase and point.

listening.text: Le garçon s'appelle François, avec un c cédille.
listening.meaning: The boy is called François, with a c cedilla.
listening.note: The cedilla makes the c sound like s.

concept.title: The hidden s
concept.markdown:
An **accent circonflexe** often marks an **s** that French lost and English kept:

- **la forêt**: forest
- **l'hôpital**: hospital
- **la fête**: feast
- **le château**: castle

Put the s back and the English word often appears.

guide.tip: Write accents on capital letters too: ÉCOLE is clearer than ECOLE, and dictionaries and official forms use them.

conversations.title: A library card
conversations.scenario: Chloé Lefèvre signs up for a card at the town library, and Julien at the desk needs her name and e-mail address.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Bonjour, madame. C'est pour une carte de bibliothèque ?
lines.meaning: Hello, madam. Is it for a library card?

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Oui, bonjour. Je m'appelle Chloé Lefèvre.
lines.meaning: Yes, hello. My name is Chloé Lefèvre.

lines.speaker: a
lines.note: ça s'écrit comment ? asks for the spelling

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: L, E, F, E accent grave, V, R, E.
lines.meaning: L, E, F, E grave accent, V, R, E.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Merci. Et Chloé, avec un e accent aigu ?
lines.meaning: Thank you. And Chloé, with an e acute accent?

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Oui : C, H, L, O, E accent aigu.
lines.meaning: Yes: C, H, L, O, E acute accent.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Parfait. Vous avez une adresse e-mail ?
lines.meaning: Perfect. Do you have an e-mail address?

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Oui : chloe point lefevre arobase mail point f r.
lines.meaning: Yes: chloe dot lefevre at mail dot f r.

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Oui, sans accent et tout en minuscules.
lines.meaning: Yes, no accent and all in lower case.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Très bien. Voilà votre carte, madame.
lines.meaning: Very good. Here's your card, madam.

bites.title: G is zhay, J is zhee
bites.rule: G is said zhay, J zhee. French E sounds like euh, I like ee. W is double v, Y is i grec, H is ash.
bites.example: Gare, ça s'écrit G, A, R, E.
bites.example_meaning: Gare is spelled G, A, R, E.

bites.title: Accents change words
bites.rule: é is a closed ay, è and ê an open eh. Où (where) is not ou (or), à (to, at) is not a (has). Ç says s before a, o, u.
bites.example_meaning: Where do you live? In Paris.

bites.title: Silent endings, nasal vowels
bites.rule: A final e and most final consonants are silent (Paris, petit); c, r, f, l are often heard. An, on, in, un are said through the nose.

bites.title: Spell it out
bites.rule: Ask Ça s'écrit comment ? Spell letter by letter: majuscule, deux l, e accent aigu, tiret. In e-mails, @ is arobase and . is point.
bites.example: Ça s'écrit avec un M majuscule.
bites.example_meaning: It's spelled with a capital M.

sorts.title: Accent aigu or accent grave?
sorts.why: é (closed ay) carries an accent aigu; è (open eh) carries an accent grave.

sorts.title: Is the last letter heard?
sorts.why: Most final consonants are silent; c, r, f and l are often heard (think CaReFuL).

sorts.title: Où or ou?
sorts.why: Où with an accent asks where; ou without one means or.

spots.why: Before o, the c needs a cedilla to sound like s: garçon.
'Where' is où, with a grave accent; ou means 'or'.
'In' before a city is à, with an accent; a is 'has'.

spots.sentence: Dans une adresse e-mail, @ se dit point.
spots.why: @ is arobase; point is the dot.
The é of été carries an accent aigu.

builds.meaning: My first name takes a capital letter.

realm.content:
## L'alphabet à Eldmark

At the guild, the scribe writes every new adventurer in the register: **Votre nom, ça s'écrit comment ?** The elf answers: **N, i grec, M.** Borin adds: **B, O, R, I, N, avec un B majuscule !** And the mage: **S, E accent aigu, L, A.**

vocabulary.example: Séla s'écrit avec un e accent aigu.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Séla is spelled with an e acute accent.

vocabulary.example: Guerrière, ça prend un accent grave.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Guerrière takes a grave accent.

vocabulary.example: Highgate prend une majuscule.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Highgate takes a capital letter.

vocabulary.example: Le nain épelle son nom pour la guilde.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The dwarf spells his name for the guild.

vocabulary.example: Borin, ça s'écrit B, O, R, I, N.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Borin is spelled B, O, R, I, N.

vocabulary.example: Le nom de la guerrière a un tiret : Lune-Rouge.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The warrior's name has a hyphen: Lune-Rouge.

vocabulary.example: Le scribe écrit les noms des héros.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The scribe writes down the heroes' names.

vocabulary.example: Ton nom est dans le registre de la guilde.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Your name is in the guild's register.

vocabulary.example: Le parchemin est écrit en majuscules.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The scroll is written in capitals.

bites.title: Chez le scribe
bites.rule: The guild's scribe asks Ça s'écrit comment ? Spell letter by letter, with accents and capitals: S, E accent aigu, L, A.
bites.example: Séla, ça s'écrit S, E accent aigu, L, A.
bites.example_meaning: Séla is spelled S, E acute accent, L, A.

listening.text: Le scribe écrit ton nom.
listening.meaning: The scribe writes down your name.
listening.note: New word: le scribe = the scribe.

listening.text: Mon nom est dans le registre.
listening.meaning: My name is in the register.
listening.note: New word: le registre = the register.

listening.text: Nym, ça s'écrit avec un i grec.
listening.meaning: Nym is spelled with a y.

listening.text: Le nain épelle son nom en majuscules.
listening.meaning: The dwarf spells his name in capitals.

listening.text: Le donjon, ça s'écrit comment ?
listening.meaning: Donjon: how is it spelled?

builds.meaning: Your name: how is it spelled?

builds.text: Nym s'écrit avec un i grec.
builds.meaning: Nym is spelled with a y.

spots.why: Guerrière takes an accent grave: the e before the final syllable is an open eh.

spots.sentence: Le nom de l'elfe prend une minuscule.
spots.why: A name always starts with a capital letter: une majuscule.

sorts.title: Majuscule or minuscule in Eldmark?
sorts.why: Names of people and places start with a majuscule; ordinary nouns are written in minuscules.

quiz.prompt: The guild's scribe writes 'Séla'. Which accent sits on its e?
quiz.explanation: É rises to the right: that's the accent aigu, and it sounds like 'ay'.
hints: The stroke on é rises to the right.

quiz.prompt: Le scribe demande : Votre nom, ça s'écrit ___ ?
quiz.explanation: Ça s'écrit comment ? = How is it spelled? Comment means 'how'.

meadowbrook.content:
## L'alphabet à Meadowbrook

At the graineterie, Rosa writes a label for each bag of seeds: **fraise**, **citrouille** (with **deux l**), **maïs** (**M, A, I tréma, S**). For the festival poster she writes **Fête des récoltes**: a **majuscule** on Fête, an **accent circonflexe** on its ê and an **accent aigu** on récoltes.

vocabulary.example: Le mot récolte prend un accent aigu.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The word récolte takes an acute accent.

vocabulary.example: Rivière, ça prend un accent grave.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Rivière takes a grave accent.

vocabulary.example: Meadowbrook prend une majuscule.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Meadowbrook takes a capital letter.

vocabulary.example: Rosa écrit fraise en minuscules.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Rosa writes fraise in lower case.

vocabulary.example: Léo épelle le nom de son bateau.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Léo spells the name of his boat.

vocabulary.example: Citrouille ? Ça s'écrit avec deux l.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Citrouille? It's spelled with two l's.

vocabulary.example: Rosa écrit une étiquette pour les graines.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Rosa writes a label for the seeds.

vocabulary.meaning: diaeresis, the two dots: ë, ï
vocabulary.example: Maïs prend un tréma sur le i.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Maïs takes two dots on the i.

vocabulary.example: Le maïs est grand en été.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The corn is tall in summer.

bites.title: Les étiquettes de Rosa
bites.rule: Rosa spells her labels with every accent: rivière (è), récolte (é), maïs (i tréma). A town's name, Meadowbrook, takes a majuscule.
bites.example: Maïs, ça s'écrit M, A, I tréma, S.
bites.example_meaning: Maïs is spelled M, A, I diaeresis, S.

listening.text: Rosa écrit une étiquette.
listening.meaning: Rosa writes a label.

listening.text: Il y a un tréma dans maïs.
listening.meaning: There are two dots in maïs.
listening.note: New word: le tréma = the two dots.

listening.text: Léo, ça s'écrit L, E accent aigu, O.
listening.meaning: Léo is spelled L, E acute accent, O.

listening.text: Citrouille s'écrit en minuscules.
listening.meaning: Citrouille is written in lower case.

listening.text: La fête des récoltes prend une majuscule.
listening.meaning: The harvest festival takes a capital letter.

builds.meaning: Citrouille is spelled with two l's.

spots.sentence: La riviere est près de la ferme.
spots.why: Rivière takes an accent grave on its second e.
Without the tréma, mais means 'but'; corn is le maïs.

sorts.title: Which accent on the farm?
sorts.why: é is an accent aigu, è an accent grave, and the two dots of ï and ë are a tréma.

quiz.prompt: Rosa writes 'maïs' on a seed label. What are the two dots on its ï called?
quiz.explanation: The two dots are le tréma: they tell you to say the a and the i apart (ma-eess). Mais without them means 'but'.
hints: They are not an accent aigu or grave.

quiz.prompt: On the festival poster, the town's name 'Meadowbrook' starts with a minuscule.
quiz.explanation: The name of a town is a proper noun, so it starts with a majuscule (capital letter): Meadowbrook.
hints: Names of places start with a capital.

rustwake.content:
## L'alphabet à Rustwake

At the antenne, the foreman Ruiz registers your radio-montre: **Ton nom, ça s'écrit comment ?** You spell it: **L, E accent aigu, O, avec un L majuscule.** Your radio address: **leo tiret fouilleur arobase dome point net**. In an address: no accents, everything in **minuscules**.

vocabulary.example: Ruiz, ça s'écrit R, U, I, Z.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Ruiz is spelled R, U, I, Z.

vocabulary.example: L'arobase est sur l'écran.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The at sign is on the screen.

vocabulary.example: Dome point net, c'est l'adresse du Dôme.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Dome dot net is the Dome's address.

vocabulary.example: Station-service prend un tiret.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Station-service takes a hyphen.

vocabulary.example: Dôme s'écrit avec une majuscule et un accent circonflexe.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Dôme is written with a capital letter and a circumflex.

vocabulary.example: Marta épelle le nom de la station.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Marta spells the name of the station.

vocabulary.example: Le code de la porte est en majuscules.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The door code is in capitals.

vocabulary.example: L'écran de la radio-montre est petit.
vocabulary.example_meaning: The wrist radio's screen is small.

vocabulary.example: Ma radio-montre a une adresse.
vocabulary.example_meaning: My wrist radio has an address.

bites.title: Sur la radio-montre
bites.rule: Spell your name for the radio list: letters, accents, majuscule. In an address, @ is arobase, . is point and - is tiret.
bites.example: leo tiret fouilleur arobase dome point net

listening.text: Ruiz épelle son nom.
listening.meaning: Ruiz spells his name.

listening.text: Il y a un écran sur la radio-montre.
listening.meaning: There's a screen on the wrist radio.

listening.text: Le code est en majuscules.
listening.meaning: The code is in capitals.
listening.note: New word: le code = the code.

listening.text: Il y a un tiret dans station-service.
listening.meaning: There's a hyphen in station-service.

listening.text: Mon adresse a une arobase et un point.
listening.meaning: My address has an at sign and a dot.

builds.meaning: The Dome takes a capital letter.

builds.text: Ruiz, ça s'écrit avec un z.
builds.meaning: Ruiz is spelled with a z.

spots.why: Dôme takes an accent circonflexe on the o.

spots.sentence: Sur la radio-montre, @ se dit tiret.
spots.why: @ is arobase; the tiret is the hyphen, -.

sorts.title: Arobase, point or tiret?
sorts.why: @ is read arobase, a dot is point and a hyphen is tiret.

quiz.prompt: Ruiz reads your radio address 'leo@dome.net' aloud. What does he say?
quiz.explanation: @ is arobase and the dot is point: leo arobase dome point net.
hints: The @ comes first, the dot second.

quiz.prompt: Station-service : ça s'écrit avec un ___ entre les deux mots.
quiz.explanation: The hyphen that joins station and service is le tiret.
hints: The French word for a hyphen.
